Figure 1 Interaction Effect between PSM and LOM on Job Satisfaction
The Case of Chinese Professionals in the Public Sector 723
Table 3 shows the results of a moderated regression analysis. Partici-
pants’ demographic variables (gender, age, and organizational tenure) 
were entered on step one as controls. Th e interaction eﬀ ect between 
LOM and PSM was signiﬁ cant (ΔR 2 = .04, ΔF (130) = 5.85, p = .02). 
We identiﬁ ed high and low LOM groups (one standard deviation 
above and below the mean) and computed one regression equation 
for each. After centering PSM and LOM scores, the regression equa-
tions for the high (M = 4.96) and the low LOM groups (M = 3.69) 
were as follows: high: Y = .73 + 1.30 * PSM; low: Y = .55 + 1.03 * 
PSM. Th e diﬀ erence in slope between the high and low LOM groups 
was signiﬁ cant (Δ slope = .27, p < .01) (see ﬁ gure 1), supporting 
hypothesis 2.

conducted on the six items with orthogonal rotation (varimax). The Kaiser-
Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure verified the sampling adequacy for the analysis,
KMO = .84 (‘‘great’’ according to Field, 2009), and all KMO values for individ-
ual items were ..78 (above acceptable limit of .5 according to Field, 2009).
Bartlett’s test of sphericity, x2(15) = 8,261.23, p < .000, indicated sufficiently
large interitem correlations for PCA. A single component had an eigenvalue
above Kaiser’s criterion of 1, that explained 56.33% of the variance (thus no
rotation was obtained). The scree plot unambiguously indicated this single
component, Whanaungatanga. Internal consistency of these items as a scale
was strong, with a Cronbach’s a = .83, and the factor loadings for items were
all sufficiently strong (ranging from .65 to .8; see Table 1).
Given the degree to which these items met conventional PCA criteria as
a scale, this analysis indicates that they can be used as a reliable measure of
Te Kotahitanga’s theorized (and qualitatively validated; Bishop et al., 2007)
conception of Whanaungatanga. Taken together as a simple summative
scale (averaged), this measure obtained a reasonably normal distribution,
with a range from 1 to 5 and a mean of 3.65 (SD = .74, SE = .01). Table 2
presents the measures of skew and kurtosis obtained indicated this roughly
normal distribution (both are very slightly negative).

large number of potential interdependencies, D8 was quite small,
with median value .0004 and a heavily right-skewed distribution.
Therefore a logarithmic transformation was applied for statistical
testing, which produced an approximately normal distribution.
Figure 7A shows untransformed means (i.e., emean(log(D8))) as a
function of focus. As shown in Table 1, there was a strong effect
of FOA (p < .01), with mean log(D8) being smaller for the
external foci. The linear contrast was marginally significant (p =
.07). There was no indication of an effect of session (p = .60; see
Table 2), although there was marginal evidence for a session–focus
interaction, F(4.79, 67.12) = 2.03, GG ε  .40, p = .09,  2  .13.
